summary: Describes a framework for using forward error correction (FEC) codes to make bulk data transfer over IP multicast more reliable. It defines what extra information must travel with the encoded data, and how new FEC codes are specified and registered with IANA. It also sets requirements for protocols that want to use these codes.

plainLanguage.summary: If you send a puzzle through the mail and some pieces get lost, extra clever spare pieces let the receiver still finish it. This document sets the rules for sending those spare pieces to many people at once.

subtitle: A framework for using forward error correction codes in reliable multicast and other content delivery protocols.

tldr.problem: Reliable bulk data delivery over IP multicast needs error correction that works with many different codes and many different delivery protocols, without each pairing needing custom design.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines FEC schemes, identified by an FEC Encoding ID, and splits the extra information into FEC Object Transmission Information and a per-packet FEC Payload ID. It then states what an FEC scheme specification and a Content Delivery Protocol specification must each contain.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes the Experimental RFC 3452 and supplies a block partitioning algorithm plus IANA registries. It gives no congestion control, so another building block must provide it.

facts.label: Congestion control
facts.value: Not provided; another building block must supply it

today: RFC 5052 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes the Experimental RFC 3452. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Goals
sections.content:
RFC 5052 describes how to use Forward Error Correction (FEC) codes to support reliable delivery of content within a Content Delivery Protocol (CDP). It is a building block in the sense of RFC 3048. Its goal is a framework where CDPs work with a range of FEC codes without knowing their details, and FEC schemes work with a range of CDPs without knowing theirs.

A CDP here may consist of several protocol mechanisms and may serve any application needing reliable transport, such as object delivery or streaming. The document also gives guidelines for writing an RFC for a new FEC scheme.

RFC 3452, which this document obsoletes, was published as Experimental, partly because suitable congestion control strategies were not yet specified. This Proposed Standard updates it with accumulated experience.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a set of rules so that many different delivery systems and many different spare-piece recipes can be mixed and matched without a special deal for each pair.

sections.title: Why FEC for Multicast
sections.content:
FEC encoding symbols are useful to every receiver for rebuilding an object even when the receivers got different symbols. FEC can also reduce or remove the need for receivers to ask the sender to retransmit lost packets. That matters for IP multicast, where one sender serves many receivers. The RFC notes FEC is also useful for unicast.

The document stays out of anything specific to one CDP or one scheme. What it covers is the definition and transport of three kinds of information from sender to receivers: the encoding symbols themselves, ancillary information about symbols or groups of symbols (such as one packet or one source block), and ancillary information about the whole object. It does not say how receivers request particular symbols.
sections.plainLanguage: One spare piece can fix a different hole for each person, so the sender does not have to answer everyone's separate complaint about a missing piece.

sections.title: FEC Schemes and Encoding IDs
sections.content:
An FEC scheme is more than a code: it defines the ancillary information and procedures that, combined with a code, fully define how the code is used with CDPs. A scheme is Fully-Specified if independent implementors can build an encoder and decoder from an IETF RFC. It is Under-Specified when no specification is available or the owner will not disclose the algorithm.

Schemes are identified by an FEC Encoding ID, an integer assigned by IANA that lets receivers select the right decoder. It MUST be the same for all transmissions of symbols of one object. An Under-Specified scheme instance is identified by the pair (FEC Encoding ID, FEC Instance ID), and that pair MUST identify one instance with at least one implementation. The owner MUST be able to say how to obtain it. The Instance ID is not used for Fully-Specified schemes.
sections.plainLanguage: Some recipes for spare pieces are published for anyone to follow, and some are secret. Every recipe gets a number so the receiver knows which one to use.

sections.title: FEC Object Transmission Information
sections.content:
The FEC Object Transmission Information (OTI) is everything the decoder needs for the whole object. It has three kinds of elements. The only Mandatory element is the FEC Encoding ID, an integer from 0 to 255. Common elements are optional for a scheme: FEC Instance ID, Transfer-Length, Encoding-Symbol-Length, Maximum-Source-Block-Length and Max-Number-of-Encoding-Symbols. A scheme may also define one Scheme-specific element, an opaque octet string to the CDP.

The CDP must transport the OTI reliably. For Common elements the CDP either carries the scheme's encoded block or defines its own encoding for each element. If it defines its own, the encoding MUST be able to represent values up to (2^16)-1 for the FEC Instance ID, (2^48)-1 for the Transfer-Length and (2^32)-1 for the others.

A scheme MUST define an encoding format for the Common elements it uses, and SHOULD use Common elements in preference to the Scheme-specific one. If a scheme does not define a Scheme-specific element, one MUST NOT be added in later versions.
sections.plainLanguage: It is the cover sheet that comes with the whole puzzle: which recipe, how big the puzzle is and how big each piece is.

sections.title: The FEC Payload ID
sections.content:
The FEC Payload ID says how the symbols in one packet relate to the object. For source symbols it says which ones they are. For repair symbols it says how they were built. It may also name a larger group, such as the source block. A data packet that carries encoding symbols MUST include an FEC Payload ID.

Usually it is a separate field in each packet, and its size SHOULD be a small fraction of the packet size. Some schemes may derive it implicitly from other packet information, but then they only suit CDPs that provide that information. For systematic codes (those where the source data appears inside the encoded data) a scheme MAY define two Payload ID formats, one for packets with only source symbols and one for packets with at least one repair symbol. A CDP wanting to support that must say which format each packet uses.
sections.plainLanguage: It is the sticker on each envelope saying which pieces are inside, so the receiver knows where they fit.

sections.title: What Scheme and CDP Specifications Must Contain
sections.content:
A new FEC scheme specification MUST give the FEC Encoding ID (registered with IANA), the type, semantics and encoding of one or two FEC Payload IDs, the type and semantics of the OTI, and an encoding format for the Common OTI elements it uses. A Fully-Specified scheme MUST also precisely define the code, so that for a given object and parameters the encoding symbol octets are uniquely determined, and describe practical encoding and decoding algorithms. Each scheme MUST be specified independently of all others, and the RFC suggests a section outline for such specifications.

A CDP specification MUST define an encoding for the Mandatory OTI element, a reliable way to carry the Mandatory, Common and Scheme-specific OTI elements, and a way to carry the FEC Payload ID with each data packet. It MAY also indicate which of two Payload ID formats a packet uses.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side gets a checklist. Recipe writers must explain their recipe and labels clearly, and delivery systems must promise to carry the cover sheet and stickers.

sections.title: Block Partitioning Algorithm
sections.content:
The RFC includes a common algorithm to split an object into source blocks that are as close to equal length as possible: some larger blocks and some smaller blocks. FEC schemes and CDPs SHOULD use it in preference to their own where appropriate. Step one derives the number of source symbols T and source blocks N from the transfer length L, the maximum source block length B and the symbol length E. Step two derives how many blocks are larger, and the length of the larger and smaller blocks.

The first I blocks have A_large symbols and the remaining N-I blocks have A_small symbols. Each symbol is E octets, except that the last symbol of the last source block may be shorter.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a fair way to cut a long loaf into slices so that no slice is much bigger than another.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
A single corrupted packet can make the decoder rebuild an object that is completely corrupted, and in multicast one bad packet near the root of the tree can reach many receivers. The RFC RECOMMENDS source authentication and integrity checking on decoded objects before delivery, for example a hash of the object with a digital signature, and a packet authentication protocol such as TESLA. It also recommends Reverse Path Forwarding checks in routers and switches. Because FEC information may come from a session description, receivers should only accept session descriptions that are authenticated.

IANA keeps a registry of FEC Encoding IDs and FEC Instance IDs. Encoding IDs 0 to 127 are for Fully-Specified schemes and 128 to 255 for Under-Specified schemes. Encoding ID assignments need IETF Consensus. Instance ID values below 65536 are scoped by an Encoding ID in the 128 to 255 range and are assigned First Come First Served.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone slips in a fake piece, the finished puzzle comes out wrong, so you should check who sent each piece and check the picture at the end.

cells: FEC Encoding ID, an integer from 0 to 255
FEC Instance ID, Transfer-Length, Encoding-Symbol-Length, Maximum-Source-Block-Length, Max-Number-of-Encoding-Symbols
One opaque octet string, structure chosen by the scheme

data.title: Block partitioning
data.code:
Step 1:  T = ceil[L/E]
         N = ceil[T/B]

Step 2:  A_large = ceil[T/N]
         A_small = floor[T/N]
         I       = T - A_small * N

First I blocks have A_large symbols;
the remaining N-I blocks have A_small symbols.
